newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Goh prestige at stake if Singapore opposition gains.
newsitem.headline: Goh prestige at stake if Singapore opposition gains.

text.p: Singapore's ruling party appeared on Tuesday to be making an all-out effort to win a key constituency, where defeat at Thursday's general election could mean a doubling of the opposition strength in parliament.

Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong staked his own prestige on his People's Action Party (PAP) winning Cheng San, a constituency in the north of Singapore, and admitted on Tuesday that victory for the opposition there would hurt him.

"I will be seen as a much smaller man," The New Paper quoted Goh as saying. "As the PM, my word in future will have less weight both internationally as well as in Singapore. I fight to win. I cannot lose."

Political analysts say Cheng San, a winner-take-all multi-member constituency with five seats at stake, may offer the left-leaning opposition Workers' Party its best chance of increasing its representation in parliament.
Victory there could double the number of opposition MPs to eight from the current four and could damage Goh's reputation as a strong and convincing leader, analysts say.
The PAP is already assured of a majority in the new 83-member parliament because opposition parties are only contesting 36 seats.
But Goh, who leads a party which faced no opposition in parliament for 13 years until 1981, has said he aims to regain all the seats and stem a recent ebb of votes away from the PAP.
"If the opposition wins eight to 10 seats, it could jeopardise Goh's premiership," said Bruce Gale, analyst at Hong Kong based Political and Economic Risk Consultancy (PERC).
"I don't see that happening...I think the opposition may win as few as two seats, but the PAP is taking no chances," he said.
The PAP trained all its big guns on Cheng San on Monday with speeches by Goh, former prime minister Lee Kuan Yew and other ministers attacking the Workers' Party challenge there.

Particular venom was reserved for Workers' Party candidate Tang Liang Hong, denounced by PAP leaders as a "Chinese chauvinist" for some of his recent comments on the need for ethnic Chinese to speak in Chinese rather than English.
Goh spent almost his entire 45-minute lunchtime speech on Monday attacking Tang, saying he was throwing his own hat into the ring to prevent Tang's election.
"I am upping the stakes," said Goh, who has already been returned unopposed in his own constituency. "I'm now stepping into the Cheng San arena. It's a contest between me and him."

Analysts said the PAP viewed Tang as the easiest target among the five Workers' Party candidates led by charismatic veteran Joshua Jeyaretnam, the first to break the PAP monopoly in parliament and who has a significant personal following.

Since electors must opt for a slate of candidates in a multi-member constituency, and cannot pick and choose which ones to vote for, discrediting one candidate could be the most effective way of reducing support for the whole group.
The Workers' Party, which has been drawing big crowds to its rallies, says the race in Cheng San is close and there have been rumours of some canvass returns showing them ahead.
A PAP source, who declined to be identified, told Reuters on Tuesday he doubted that was true: "There is no evidence for that. We'll probably win," he said.
But Goh wants to be certain of victory in Cheng San.
"After all, Goh has said, it would undermine him if he couldn't maintain the PAP hegemony," said Gale. "I think it could change the political climate significantly."
Chia Woon Khien, economist at Union Bank of Switzerland in Singapore, said she had seen no evidence to suggest the governing party would suffer any major defeat on Thursday.

"I think the PAP's vote will be close to the last election when they got 61 percent of the votes cast," Chia said. "I don't think it is possible, but if the PAP vote fell to under 50 percent, Goh might have to go."
